title: Measured lexicographic witness production across different witness lengths
claims: A measured order-preserving word encoding lets the sparse truth-table witness machine return the lexicographically first accepted witness even when accepted lengths differ.
Under the bounded sparse truth-table hypothesis, a reference polynomial-time machine outputs a shortest accepted witness for any polynomially bounded relation, breaking ties lexicographically.

Under a fixed-arity truth-table reduction from an NP-hard language to a sparse target, the new reference machine returns the lexicographically least accepted exact-length witness, or explicit failure.
A measured parameterized selector returns the last matching word in an encoded frontier with a success tag.
The variable truth-table and constant-round adaptive conditional collapse theorems now derive decision from the directed pruning and witness machine.
A measured variable-table pruner uses two query restrictions per fiber, then retains only the required side of each all-false-entry group.
The directed recurrence is bounded by 2^k times the fixed-table recurrence and is no larger than the full-table grouping bound for every arity.
The exact one-sided boundary lemma proves the false-default prefix and true-default suffix guarantees, including the zero budget.
A pinned polynomial-time fixed-round adaptive reduction from an NP-hard or coNP-hard language to a cumulatively sparse target implies P = NP.
For each fixed answer assignment, the transcript compiler measures the leaf computation and proves the correct adaptive transcript using exact query indices.
For fixed arity, an encoded polynomial-time truth-table reduction from an NP-hard language to a cumulatively polynomially sparse target implies P = NP.
The measured pruning machine handles a different Boolean truth table at each candidate and preserves every valid last-true boundary of the same frontier.
The fixed-table pruner has a verified polynomial width bound and only uses the encoded candidates and unary sparse count.
The ordered frontier solver uses reference polynomial-time machines for fixed-depth binary witness expansion, certified pruning and terminal verification.
The pinned P subset NP theorem checks independently.
